implementation_notes: The JDK ships the pattern for collections: CopyOnWriteArrayList is 'a thread-safe variant of ArrayList in which all mutative operations (add, set, and so on) are implemented by making a fresh copy of the underlying array', and its iterator is a snapshot - 'the iterator will not reflect additions, removals, or changes to the list since the iterator was created' - so traversal needs no lock and cannot throw ConcurrentModificationException. The package guide states the rule that keeps it honest: 'A CopyOnWriteArrayList is preferable to a synchronized ArrayList when the expected number of reads and traversals greatly outnumber the number of updates to a list.' What replaces the counted body is the JVM's safe publication over the array reference: there is no user-visible reference count to protect and the copy is paid per mutation. For whole-value state instead of a list, the second variant publishes an immutable snapshot through an AtomicReference.
pitfalls: The copy is per mutation, not per transaction: add/set/removeAll each copy the whole backing array, so a write-heavy list degenerates into O(n) copies and garbage - ConcurrentLinkedQueue or ConcurrentHashMap are the right shapes there.

Snapshot iterators never see later changes and iterator.remove/set/add throw UnsupportedOperationException: code that relied on a live view or on in-place removal must be restructured (iterate to collect, then removeAll).

The collection is thread-safe, the elements are not: a mutable Listener or value stored inside still needs its own synchronisation, and compound check-then-act sequences on the list need an external lock.

variants.name: AtomicReference-published immutable snapshot
variants.implementation_notes: When the shared state is a whole value rather than a list, publish an immutable snapshot through one reference: AtomicReference is 'an object reference that may be updated atomically' whose get/set have volatile memory effects, and its functional updateAndGet/accumulateAndGet retry the transformation until the compare-and-set wins, so a reader either sees the snapshot before or after an update and never a partial one. Java 10's List.copyOf/Map.copyOf/Set.copyOf produce the immutable snapshot cheaply to build once and share. That replaces the counted body with the JVM's safe publication: readers hold their own local reference to the snapshot they read, writers copy-on-write and publish. Same caution as the collection variant - the copy is per update, so it fits read-mostly state.
pitfalls: updateAndGet may invoke the lambda several times: it must be side-effect-free and derive the new snapshot only from the value it is handed, or a retried update duplicates its effect.

Map.copyOf is shallow: a mutable value inside the snapshot is shared with every reader, and a reference to the mutable map that was copied still aliases nothing - so deep-immutability is the caller's job.
Copying a large map per update is O(n) and the CAS loop is not starvation-free: for write-heavy state ConcurrentHashMap (fine-grained locking) beats snapshot publishing.
